author: David Wildstein
title: Sherrill launches group to tackle rising public employee health costs - New Jersey Globe
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill is launching a broad working group to recommend changes to New Jersey’s public employee health benefits system, bringing unions, health care providers, insurers, local government groups, and lawmakers together to control rising costs.
The State Health Benefits Program Reform Working Group, led by Sherrill Chief Operating Officer Kellie Doucette, will hold its first meeting on October 16 and is expected to develop recommendations for the governor to make the system more affordable and financially sustainable.
The move fulfills a commitment Sherrill made last month as part of an agreement with 17 unions representing state employees.
“From Day One, I have been focused on making New Jersey more affordable, and that means tackling hard problems instead of kicking them down the road,” Sherrill said. “Rising healthcare costs affect public employees and retirees, the local governments and schools that serve our communities, and taxpayers across the state.”
Sherrill said the state has historically dealt with health benefit costs “one rate cycle at a time” and said the new effort would instead examine longer-term structural changes.
“We are taking a different approach by bringing stakeholders together, working from shared data, and pursuing long-term changes that preserve high-quality benefits while making these programs more affordable and sustainable,” she said.
The working group will examine how the state administers public employee health benefits, provider networks and reimbursement, plan pricing and employee premium contributions, benefit design, participation by employers and employees, and the governance and information systems used to manage the programs.
Separate subcommittees will conduct more detailed reviews of those areas and bring in additional experts and stakeholders.
“The challenges facing public employee health benefits demand that same approach,” Doucette said. “We look forward to working collaboratively to build a road map for systemic reform, using all of the levers available to us and focusing not just on the what but on the how; understanding that a plan for implementation is as important as the recommendations themselves.”
Doucette said the goal is to produce “measurable results that employees, employers, and taxpayers deserve.”
The group includes more than two dozen labor organizations, among them the Communications Workers of America, AFSCME, the New Jersey AFL-CIO, police and firefighter unions, Rutgers AAUP-AFT and Teamsters Joint Council 73.
Health care participants include the New Jersey Hospital Association, Medical Society of New Jersey, New Jersey State Nurses Association and New Jersey Association of Health Plans.
The state’s current health benefit vendors — Aetna, Horizon Blue Cross Blue Shield of New Jersey and Optum Rx — will also participate.
Local government and education interests will be represented by groups including the New Jersey State League of Municipalities, New Jersey Association of Counties, New Jersey School Boards Association, New Jersey Conference of Mayors and New Jersey Association of School Administrators.
All four partisan legislative offices — the Senate and Assembly Democratic and Republican offices — are also represented.
The group’s recommendations will be advisory, leaving Sherrill to determine which proposals to pursue.
New Jersey operates separate health benefit programs covering state workers, local government employees and school employees, with different plans, governing structures and legal requirements. The administration said the new working group will coordinate its work with separate efforts involving the Local Government Group and School Employees’ Health Benefits Program.
That distinction could matter because the group’s recommended changes cannot necessarily be imposed on all public employees. Depending on the proposal, implementation could require collective bargaining, administrative or procurement actions, approval by benefits commissions, legislation or other legal processes.
The administration also plans to bring in organizations and experts who are not formal members of the working group as the review progresses.
After its October 16 organizational meeting, the group will meet regularly to develop and prioritize recommendations for Sherrill. More detailed work on designing and implementing any changes is expected to continue into 2027.
